body: We are asking the questions, we are lying to get by We are lying on our backs, wondering about the sky We are blind when it suits us, we still hear the noise Are these delusions of our making? Is this the illusion of choice? Every life eventually arrives at the same locked door: the one behind which the meaning of it all is supposed to be waiting. As the years burn, we gather love, pleasure, machines, money, memories, and little mementos of our existence, only to find the old questions still standing there, untouched, and unanswered. With “All We’ve Known of Heaven,” Soft Vein turns that existential ache into a sleek new wave confession, one lit by bright synths, bruised romance, and the uneasy knowledge that abundance does not always equal salvation. The second single from his forthcoming new album continues Justin Chamberlain’s recent evolution into a more refined, sophisticated synthpop silhouette. Where earlier Soft Vein material often leaned heavily into darkwave gloom, “All We’ve Known of Heaven” moves with a more cinematic sense of yearning: a sighing, almost church-like introduction opening into a pulsing bass synth, rippling electronics, and a breathy vocal performance that feels suspended between confession. The song follows the previously released single Chekov in placing Chamberlain’s voice and writing at the center. The production, co-produced by Chamberlain with Andrea Mantione of Nuovo Testamento, has the sheen of expensive glass and the anxiety of someone staring straight through it. There is an unmistakable 1980s charge here: a nocturnal, Michael Mann-like glow; the elegant propulsion of new wave pop; and vocal harmonies that call to mind the grand emotional sweep of Simple Minds without slipping into too much of their new gold sheen. Lyrically, “All We’ve Known of Heaven” circles the elegant catastrophes of modern life: desire, consumption, spiritual exhaustion, the little betrayals people commit simply to keep moving. The song asks what remains when everything has been acquired except meaning. Its central question — “Is this all we are?” — becomes less a cry of defeat than a flare sent into the cogs of our disconnected digital existence, in search of a sign of life beyond our modern appetites and illusions. That tension gives the track its strange pull. Soft Vein writes about a world in which modern convenience has multiplied beyond imagination — machines for pleasure, endless means of contact, every appetite fed on command — yet we seem no closer to one another, and no nearer to knowing anything like heaven. The song understands excess as both seduction and trap: the comfort that dulls us, the desire that divides us, the little betrayals people commit while searching for warmth in the wrong rooms. By the time Rachel Mazer’s saxophone arrives near the finale, it feels like a final flare of feeling inside all that machinery: romantic, wounded, and gone almost as soon as it appears. Mastered by Jason Corbett of ACTORS, “All We’ve Known of Heaven” suggests a Soft Vein expanding in real time, stepping further into an 80s pop architecture while keeping a darkwave pulse beating beneath the floorboards. There is a compelling parallel in Producer Phil Thornalley’s own arc, from the Gothic depths of The Cure’s Pornography era to the gleaming new wave heights of Johnny Hates Jazz. For Soft Vein, that kind of range does not feel like a contradiction or retreat, but the natural continuum of any good artist: a movement from severity to sophistication, from dread to desire, from the basement to the bright lights without losing the ache underneath. _cn_summary: Soft Vein 是一位在华语独立/电子圈活跃的新 wave 音乐人/团队，此前以细腻的合成器流行与后朋克氛围在现场演出中积累了不少口碑。最新单曲《All We’ve Known of Heaven》以低沉贝斯、飘渺的合成垫底搭配失真人声，在渐进式编曲中释放层次分明的回响，兼具冷冽的新 wave 质感与氛围音乐的空间感。歌词聚焦现代都市的存在焦虑与“选择之门”的隐喻，结合模拟合成器与数字处理的交叉制作手法，为华语新 wave 注入了哲思深度并提供了现场与录音版的多重情绪层次。

body: Review by siLLy puPPy — The Basque culture that straddles the northeastern part of Spain and southwestern region of Francehas fascinated linguists and anthropologists alike owing to the fact that this culture appears to beone of the last remnants of Paleolithic Europe before the arrival of the Indo-Europeans. Given thisculture's rather isolate position in terms of its relationship amongst other European cultures, it'slittle wonder that it too has developed some of its own unique musical styles. While little known tothe outside world, the Basque region did indeed participate in the flavorful sounds that emergedduring the psychedelic and progressive years and thanks to DJ Makala who compiled a number of tracksfrom various artists, this excellent compilation is like a box of assorted chocolates awaiting yourdiscovery.KATEBEGIAK Prog-Rock, Psych-Folk & Jazz-Rock Music from the Basque Country was released in 2021 andhighly acclaimed for showcasing some of the region's history that was the crucial link thatconnected the folk revivalists of the 1960s and the Basque Radical Rock (Euskal Herriko rockerradikala) that fueled the regions punk scene. The term KATEBEGIAK actually means "Links of achain." The album features 13 select tracks that display the wide array of experimental sounds thatsprang up in the 1970s and continued into the 80s. After the 60s revival movement, bands began tocross-pollinate their homegrown folk music with the various forms of psychedelia, rock and jazzfusion that were springing up all around Europe and the world since the mid-1960s and this Whitman'ssample pack is the perfect place to dip in and get a taste of such sounds for further exploration.This release features all the expected artists such as the most popular Basque act Itoiz as well asHaizea, Enbor and Errobi but also features some of the rarest of the rare with bands such as thePamplona based Magdalena and the virtually unknown Urria. Strangely this collection features arather interesting choice of what to include and what not as it features the track "Pello Joxepe"which as an outlier from rest and features a Mississippi born black psychedelic soul singer coveringa traditional Basque song and yet the release doesn't include real Basque acts that existed at thetime including Sakre, Akelarre, Mirotz and Patxi Villamor. Track lengths vary considerably as wellranging from the 3 1/2 minute "Agurra II" from Enbor to the longest track "Andere" from Errobi whichsprawls out to 13 1/2 minutes. While these acts varied widely in approach, the thread that keeps it all connected is the softsensual folk and oft flute oriented music that in some ways resembles Celtic folk music but soundsas distinct as the language this unique population has kept alive despite all odds. Some of thetrack placements are a bit odd as the opening "Egunaren Hastapena" by Haizea takes a good fiveminutes to slowly work up to some sort of song structure. The following "Xori Bele" by Izkaitzwould've been a better choice as it provides a more direct introduction into the culturalsmorgasbord about to be experience however this is hardly a deal breaker as all the tracks areworthy of an attentive listen. While most of these artists are clearly more in the psychedelic folk camp with touches of prog rockin for the mix, bands like Lisker actually deliver the more rocking bravado whereas the tracks byAmala Zubrina & Pascual Gaigne along with the album's closer by Urria are extremely ethereal and themost experimental. Despite the urge to play these in a different order it's the music that countsand although i've heard of many of these bands i haven't actually heard them so this is the perfectway to get acquainted as well as finding some rarities that have completely escaped the attention ofeven the most sleuth oriented databases. The Basque scene was quite distinct from the Rock Andaluzand jazz fusion scenes of the rest of Spain and this compilation is the perfect way to explore thisoften neglected region of the nation. Pretty much every track works for me however i wish theexcluded acts were on this one too.
_cn_summary: 这张收录1972至1985年巴斯克地下乐团作品的《KATEBEGIAK》合集，聚焦前卫摇滚、民谣迷幻与爵士摇滚三种风格，展现当地艺术家在语言与政治压力下以本土语言创作的大胆实验。专辑保留原始低保真录音质感，巧妙融合传统巴斯克乐器（如txalaparta）与合成器、爵士即兴，形成从简约民谣到宏大交响式结构的多元听感。作为2021年汇编，它提供罕见的首版曲目与系统性注释，是研究巴斯克独立音乐史及欧洲边缘prog‑rock的重要资料。

body: Review by siLLy puPPy — After delivering a fairly unadulterated slice of traditional Basque folk music on its debut, HAIZEAjoined the late 70s craze of incorporating elements of 70s prog and 60s psychedelia into its mix andin the process took a huge leap with a substantially more adventurous and explorative sophomorerelease. On HONTZ GAUA which is Basque for "Night of the Owl," guitarist / vocalist Txomin Artolaleft the group in pursuit of a solo career and in his place flautist and guitarist Xabier Iriondojoined the ranks and helped usher HAIZEA into much more progressive territories with its set of fivetracks that only added up to just over 33 minutes. A much more avant-garde album, HONTZ GAUA wasbuilt around the same traditional Basque folk melodies of the debut only embellished with moreethereal atmospheric effects, less rigid compositional structures and extended excursions that wereinspired by the European progressive rock of the 1970s.The opening track belies the album's ambitious nature with a rather tame traditional approach."Anderea" sounds like a leftover from the previous album but starting with the second track"Egunaren Hastapena" the band blossoms quite quickly into a darker tone with less predictable songstructures all the while the feminine charm of Amala Zubira takes on a darker at times even gothicapproach sounding something like if Sandy Denny was auditioning for Dead Can Dance. Althoughprimarily acoustic in nature, electric guitars are used more liberally this time around withpsychedelic dressing applied to tracks like "Argizagi Ederra" to great affect as well asincorporating more demanding time signature approaches rather than untempered guitar chordstrumming. Irondo adds a lot of intricate flute moments as well as adding the distinguished tones ofthe Portuguese guitar. "Arnaki" offers a twin guitar effect which takes the music into a 60spsychedelic vibe.Once again all lyrics are in the Basque language which offers a unique rhythmic flow unlike any ofthe Romance languages and therefore sounds quite distinct from the Rock Andaluz acts that wereflooding Spain in the 70s. Touches of jazz are incorporated for musical textures but nothing in thefusion sense ever intrudes on the rather subdued psychedelic light-hearted nature of the album evenwhen the twin electric guitars are at the most feisty. The jewel in the crown is the side long titletrack broken down into two distinct segments which at over 14 minutes offer plenty of excursionsinto true unrestricted progressive territories. Beginning with a Gregorian chant followed by abaptizing water sound effect sequence before gently rolling out the flute and acoustic guitar beforethe ethereal vocal harmonies kick in. Tender percussion is added and the track oozes around quicklyskillfully as it shape shifts through various musical motifs steeped in heavy psychedelic effectswith some sort of chimes and intricate changes through varying passages. Easily the best track ofthe band's career.The light airy feel of the album laced with beautiful melodies and adventurous performances in anexotic language may make you feel like you've drifted away into some far away land as HAIZEAaugments its Basque folk traditions into powerful psychedelic folk statements. Laced withtraditional wind instruments and various percussive techniques, HONTZ GAUA adds a sense of darknessliving up to its title meaning of "Night of the Owl." Zubiria delivers an excellent display of vocalcontrol evolving beyond her cutsie good girl folk style of the debut and the icing on the cake arethe explorative shifts in song structure that feel organically natural and not hastily thrown intothe mix. A guest violinist delivers some serous melancholy and band displayed a remarkable maturityon this sophomore offering most likely due to the fact much time was spent the previous yearsbetween albums on the live circuit and best of all the band seriously integrated the progcharacteristics perfectly. A charming mellow album that is one of the highlights of the Basqueinfused prog folk craze of the era.
_cn_summary: HAIZEA 是一支根植于巴斯克传统民谣的乐队，1979 年的第二张专辑《Hontz Gausa》（意为“夜枭之夜”）标志着他们将民谣与 70 年代前卫摇滚及 60 年代迷幻音乐融合，形成鲜明的 prog‑folk 风格。吉他/人声 Txomin Artola 离队后，乐团引入长笛手和新吉他手，使作品在保持巴斯克旋律根基的同时拥有了更丰富的层次感、实验性编排以及长笛飘渺的音色。整张专辑兼具温暖的民谣旋律与复杂的前卫节奏，是探索巴斯克音乐与现代摇滚融合不可错过的亮点之作。

body: Review by martindavey87 — Black Sabbath's aptly titled 'Vol. 4' is the British metal pioneers' fourth studio album, and once again, it's another release that I struggle to really get into. I don't dislike Black Sabbath, I enjoy most genres of music and most bands, from any era. But for whatever reason, the stars just do not align because I just don't "get" the first few Black Sabbath albums. I'm sure there's a point, perhaps later in their career, where the band just clicks with me, but their first few records, often revered as metal masterpieces by fans, just do nothing for me. It's not all gloom and doom though (well, it kind of is!), as there are a couple of highlights. 'Snowblind' is a fantastic song, probably ranking up there as one of my Sabbath favourites, cheesy ballad 'Changes' has some great vocal and lyrics, and 'St. Vitus Dance' has some interesting guitar work. But overall, I find the rest of the tracks just seem to plod along, similarly to how I felt about their previous releases. I've tried and tried, and have had this one on my playlist for a while, but it's just not working for me. Perhaps I'll have more luck with their next album?
_cn_summary: 1972年发行的《Volume 4》是英国重金属先驱Black Sabbath的第四张专辑，标志着乐队在《Paranoid》《Master of Reality》之后向更具实验性的音乐结构迈进。专辑中最突出的听感是Tony Iommi低沉的降调失真吉他、Bill Ward厚重的双踩鼓点以及在《Wheels of Confusion》《Supertzar》等曲中首次使用的合成器和相位/混响效果，形成重金属冲击与渐进摇滚结构的交织。《Sweet Leaf》的蓝调慢riff与《Children of the Grave》《Tomorrow’s Dream》的高能riff形成强烈对比，展现了乐队在保持金属核心的同时对旋律与编曲的大胆探索，因而被视为早期重金属与前卫金属融合的里程碑。

body: Review by martindavey87 — Let's just be honest here, does anyone actually go out of their way to listen to this album? The thing is, it's not bad, it's just, well? weird. 'Time Requiem', a progressive metal band specializing in lightning-fast flurries of notes in a neoclassical vein, is the product of keyboard mastermind Richard Andersson. They'd only released one studio album prior to this, so like? why produce a live album so early in their career?It just seems unusual. I don't know a lot about the band, but I would take a guess that, like other, similar groups, they probably don't gig very often, if ever. And with a limited choice of songs, it just doesn't really offer much for the listener to sink their teeth into. For what it's worth though, the performances are fantastic. Each member of the band plays with machine-like precision. The sound is very good, and the crowd seem quite receptive to the band, though my guess is that this isn't typically a Time Requiem audience. It could also just be that I've always preferred studio albums to their live counterparts. But overall, this isn't a bad release, but I doubt I'll ever listen to it again. I'll just stick to the bands studio output instead.
_cn_summary: Time Requiem 是瑞典键盘手 Richard Andersson 主导的新古典速弹派前卫金属项目，2004 年的现场专辑《Unleashed in Japan》在日本录制，展现了乐团自首张专辑仅一年后即以现场形式记录其极具技术性的演奏。专辑以极快的键盘独奏与锋利的吉他速弹交织为核心，音色偏重新古典主义的炫技段落，同时保留现场的热烈氛围与冲击力。值得注意之处在于，这张 Live 作品虽在乐团发展早期发行，却已呈现出高水平的演奏默契与现场冲击力，是乐迷了解 Andersson 键盘技巧和日本现场氛围的理想窗口。

body: Review by TenYearsAfter — Ruud Dielen had a long history with cover bands , playing guitar in songs from Jimi Hendrix, Santana, Led Zeppelin, Queen, Toto and Genesis. After many years touring in the more commercial circuit, he decided that it was time to write his own music and in 2017 he produced his first album entitled Aquarius, as a one-man-band (guitar, bass and synthesizers), under the name Glorious Wolf. The music sounds as a tribute to the Seventies era progrock and Classic Rock, from Pink Floyd to Zappa and Hendrix, embellished with a wonderful array of vintage sounds (from Moog, Mellotron and Hammond to Gibson, Fender and Mesa Boogie). On his second album Zodiac (2019) and third Mysterious Traveller (2023) Ruud started to invite male and female singers, and to blend the progrock sound with a more song-oriented and varied musical attitude. On Prog Archives Ruud Dielen his Glorious Wolf project got a lot of praise for that musical formula, meandering tastefully and elaborately between instrumental Old School vintage keyboard drenched progrock and song-oriented tracks. And now, anno 2026, here's Ruud again (playing acoustic - and electric guitars, fretless bass, Precision bass, synthesizers, mellotron and FX drums) with Glorious Wolf, featuring a range of national and international guest musicians, on vocals, drums, bass, Hammond, Yamaha piano, Mellotron, theremin and saxophone. Most of the foreign musicians Ruud had met during an international musical collaboration.Elements of Hope Pt.1 ? Instrumental (4.34) : This new album starts with an exciting electronic music atmosphere featuring pulsating sequencers and spacey synthesizers, then howling and biting Gilmourian guitar runs, topped with Mellotron choirs, followed by a tight and catchy beat. The music is embellished with Ruud his powerful guitar runs, fat synthesizer flights and soaring Mellotron choirs, and backed by a fluent rhythm-section (Kike Paglia on drums and Tim Ros on bass). In the end majectic Mellotron choirs erupt, wow, what an impressive start!Elements of Hope Pt.2 - Carrying this Yoke (6.15) : The intro delivers psychedelic sounding Mellotron violins. The music turns into a folky climate with acoustic guitar and fragile English male vocals (by Frank van der Borg), in a slow rhythm. Gradually a more lush sound featuring Mellotron violins, and powerful vocals and guitar riffs. In the final part a break with raw guitar riffs and propulsive drum beats. Lots of contrast, variety and dynamics, and tastefully arranged.Elements of Hope Pt.3 - Into the Clouds (5.55) : First celestial female vocals (by Jyoti Verhoeff) and twanging acoustic guitar, in a dreamy and hypnotizing climate, wonderful. Now the sound becomes more lush, embellished with fretless bass, slow drumbeats and distinctive female vocals. Gradually the atmosphere is working to a symptuous climax with a synthesizer solo, powerful drums and Hammond, culminating into fiery guitar solo, how exciting.Elements of Hope Pt.4 ? Instrumental (1.42) : A short piece in an ominous climate, with raw and powerful guitar, and slow and powerful drumbeats, the interplay is awesome.Elements of Hope Pt.5 - Life's Chaotic Spell (5.51) : The final part of this 5-pieve epic title track contains omnipresent Hammond, blended with exciting rock guitar, powerful male English vocals and a propulsive rhythm-section. Now saxophone play (by Reg Parham) joins, strongly coloring the music, with hints from Frank Zappa and King Crimson. Finally a heavy guitar solo, backed by a dynamic rhythm-section and Hammond.If You Please ? instrumental (6.20) : This composition delivers a slow rhythm and a compelling climate, Ruud really shines with his guitarwork, from sensitive to fiery, and using the tremolo-arm and wah-wah pedal, prog meets bluesrock, wow. Halfway beeps and bleeps, then a more atmospheric sound featuring spectacular wah-wah driven guitar runs, backed by propulsive drumbeats.If I Only (5.46) : After an intro with Mellotron (by the late Thomas Zunk) and militairy drums the music turns into a slow rhythm with heavy guitar, strong male vocals and gradually a more bombastic atmosphere. Halfway a fiery guitar solo, with howling and biting leads and Hammond layers, the music builds and builds, very compelling and exciting.Whirlwinds & Maelstroms ? instrumental (6.44) : Another Mellotron soaken intro, then slow drumbeats and powerful guitar. Halfway a swirling Hammond solo (XK5 Hammond with Leslie by Harry Knapen), followed by a heavy guitar solo, the interplay is excellent.Everything Must Break to Grow - EoH Pt.2 Reprise (6.25) : The final track on this new album starts with dreamy piano and vocals, then a slow rhythm, in a melancholical atmosphere, topped with subtle slide guitar. Gradually the sound turns into more lush and powerful featuring rock guitar and a dynamic rhythm-section. Finally dreamy with spacey synthesizers, guitar and voices, another example of Ruud his interesting and varied musical ideas.In the 3 years after his previous effort Ruud has moved and built a high-tec studio in his new home. You can hear the result: a mature and elaborate new album on which the music is wonderfully meandering between Old School prog and a more varied and song-oriented musical approach, embellished with his awesome guitarwork, vintage keyboards and vocal leads, and backed by good musicians. After Edo Spanninga (as E.D.O.) with his solo album The Past Is A Foreign Country, his other project Trion with Terra Tiempo here is another excellent new Dutch prog effort, well done Ruud!
_cn_summary: 荷兰吉他手Ruud Dielen在多年翻唱Jimi Hendrix、Santana、Led Zeppelin、Genesis等经典摇滚与prog作品后，2017年发行首张个人专辑《Aquarius》开启 solo 创作，2026年以 Glorious Wolf 名义推出《Elements of Hope》——一张跨界的 Crossover Prog 作品，核心是致敬70年代 prog‑rock 与 Classic Rock 的吉他‑合成器交织。专辑以强劲的电吉他即兴、层次丰富的合成器铺陈以及紧凑的结构变化为特征，兼具复古的厚重感和前卫的动态冲击，听感兼具旋律性与技术性。Dielen 将多年现场对 Hendrix、Santana、Genesis 等大师的演绎经验转化为独特的动机与即兴亮点，值得 prog 爱好者与复古摇滚乐迷关注。

body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Empath' is undoubtedly one of the most eclectic and unbridled albums Devin Townsend has everrecorded. Conceived as some sort of magnum opus, this 2019 release encompasses a diverse range ofmusical influences from the Canadian musician's extensive back catalogue - everything from blastingavant-garde metal and progressive rock to symphonic music, ambient, and dance-pop (well, the lastone is a bit ironic, but you get the picture) is part of this ambitious and maximalist progexcursion. A huge, bold, and resonant work of art, 'Empath' is to my understanding a celebration ofthe musical universe of Devin Townsend, with all of its quirky, corny, overblown and elementalfacets. Joined by co-produced Mike Keneally, this record features a rather impressive set of guestmusicians and contributors, too, including the likes of Adam "Nolly" Getgood of Periphery who isresponsible for engineering and mixing the album, drummer Morgan �gren of Kaipa who has somesongwriting credits, and Steve Vai, among many others, who contributes a flamboyant guitar solo atthe very end of the album.Made up of ten album tracks, each song on 'Empath' explores a particular corner of the DevinTownsend sound. Opener 'Genesis', with its prelude 'Castaway', is a quirky piece of prog rock withcomplex, wacky arrangements, heavy guitars and a string of surprising sounds, and for many one ofthe most representative Devin pieces on this album. 'Spirits Will Collide' then follows up with abeautifully orchestrated triumphant sound, while the fourth track 'Evermore' marks a return to thedense and heavy sound that we're more familiar with. Stylistically, this song reminisces theuplifting prog metal Townsend had explored on his 2009 album 'Addicted'. We then have the excellent'Sprite', which is one of the more experimental entries on 'Empath', combining seamlessly electronicsynth sounds with winding symphonic music. 'Hear Me' is a manic piece of metal (think of SYL as areference), and unlike the classically-inspired song 'Why?', captures one of the most maximalist DTperformances on this record. The 11-minute-long 'Borderlands', which is the next major highlight, isa really playful piece of energetic prog metal, only followed by the six-part suite 'Singularity',sitting at twenty-three-plus minutes of playtime. Featuring a string of complex shifts and thetypical Wall of sound style of production, this is one of the most powerful and angular epicsrecorded by Townsend, and while parts of it are really impressive, I would hardly call it theperfect epic as it can occasionally feel a bit too hectic and immense.Nevertheless, 'Empath' is a fabulous solo album from Devin Townsend that aims to represent the all-encompassing nature of his music, uniting together on the same record the full range of musicalinfluences that make up his world. Surely one of the impressive and memorable releases of 2019.
_cn_summary: Devin Townsend 是加拿大跨流派实验金属/前卫摇滚乐手，以技术性重型与柔和氛围兼具的多面创作著称。《Empath》（2019）全长约84分钟的双碟结构，将前卫金属、渐进摇滚、交响编制、环境音景乃至电子流行等多元风格紧密交织；如《Spiral》在凶猛金属段落后突现电子流行旋律，《Catharsis》以壮阔交响与高速金属形成强烈冲击，配合约70人管弦乐团、40人合唱团以及多位客座乐手，使整张专辑在音色层次和情绪起伏上极具冲击力与可听性。

body: Review by Fercandio46 — The third and final part of Gong's Radio Gnome Invisible trilogy, where Zero, the hero, receives his cosmic ascension, activating his third eye...deserved an imposing musical framework, befitting the importance of the events narrated. This volume thus became the most musically daring, the most experimental, and the one with the longest tracks. While each part was unique in its own way...and Angel's Egg had innovated with the short duration of its tracks and yet all its stylistic variety, You further developed these concepts, taking them a step further and becoming a classic not only for the band but for the genre itself.As the cover promises...there's a mix of spacey atmosphere and indigenous mysticism in Thoughts for Naught, Daevid Allen's composition, his ability to draw the rest into his universe...Tim Blake's synthesizers and Mike Howlett's bass in Magick Mother Invocation, creating that spacey psychedelia that always starts slowly...Didier Malherbe's saxophone, Gilli Smyth's vocals, and of course Pierre and Beno�t Moerlen's drums and percussion...plus Steve Hillage's ineffable and unmistakable guitar...everything will conspire to make that conjunction of stars explode in this volume.Master Builder is the construction of that curtain of synthesizers and the Buddhist choir...the percussion, the flute in an oriental orchestra...until the drums introduce the saxophone and the space rock jam...the cosmic French psychedelic free jazz begins...you can smell the 70s...you can feel it...there is precision, there is technique...yes...but there is also madness, freedom, anarchy, bohemianism, and that mix is ​​what made this Gong so special, ultimately, Allen's invocatory presence. When Hillage begins to play...nobody was prepared for that cascade of sound...for those doors that open in the mind with the notes of his sound...which, supported by the synthesizer, the drums and the bass, will make history.You is an album that wasn't rushed...in a decade that seized control of time to do with it as it saw fit for artistic purposes...and if this meant accelerating it to the point of confusion like King Crimson on Red...or slowing it down to the point of despair...like Gentle Giant on Free Hand...there was no doubt they were going to do it, and Gong took the time to build each step of ascent on You...because they knew that the feeling of climbing step by step is not the same as skipping steps in pursuit of a rush that only speaks of detachment from things.As layers of synthesizers build upon the drums in A Sprinkling of Clouds, and the drums with each hit seem to leap from the speakers and reach us as only a few records can...and the guitar sounds wild yet clean at the same time and you can follow its path at every moment...when Didier Malherbe joins in we understand why they distanced themselves from anyone who could do something similar and Frank Zappa's Inca's Roads didn't end up going in the same direction either.Perfect Mystery revisits the cabaret atmosphere of Angel's Egg only as a connection within the story, that oriental atmosphere that sets the stage for The Isle of Everywhere, one of the album's central themes...where synthesizers, Gilli Smyth's vocals, bass, and drums create an atmosphere reminiscent of King Crimson's Islands...only to then turn around and take another route, because Mike Howlett's swing on the bass had the necessary propulsion to soar without sopranos...and Gong sometimes has the ability to pass the third eye to us, if we can connect with his music; it's jazz...it's progressive rock...it's funk...it's psychedelia...it's the Canterbury scene, born in part because an Australian couldn't return to England and had to stay in France.Steve Hillage's solo begins so subtly behind the saxophone...but it does define itself throughout the entire development, supported by the bass and drums, at times playing with parts of jazz rock, until You Never Blow Your Trip Forever encompasses everything heard so far in the trilogy, even more psychedelic if possible...until it settles as if unintentionally into a section that, from improvised and played, culminates in another inspired song/prayer to the universe...a mantra repeated and destined to fade away, the complete opposite of this third volume of the most classic Gong which, as if it were a loop in time...must be repeated again and again once it has already ended.
_cn_summary:
GONG是一支起源于法国、受英国坎特伯雷音乐圈影响的跨世代前卫摇滚/迷幻爵士融合乐团。  
1974年的《You (Radio Gnome Invisible Vol. 3)》作为三部曲的终章，以最具实验性的结构和最长的曲目著称，融合自由即兴、合成器空间音效、长段渐进式编排以及带有神话色彩的叙事，展现了Daevid Allen等人标志性的“宇宙喜剧”风格与爵士‑摇滚‑电子的跨界混搭。  
这张专辑是70年代前卫乐迷不可错过的里程碑，其大胆的音场与叙事深度在当时的摇滚界独树一帜。

_cn_summary: 《Jaywalkin’》是丹麦低音提琴巨匠尼尔斯‑亨宁·厄斯特·佩德森（Niels‑Henning Ørsted Pedersen）在七十年代的录音，延续他以旋律性低音独奏和灵活和声语言著称的气质。专辑属后波普主流爵士，低音主导的段落结构严谨、节奏稳健，但在曲目《Cheryl》上出现的两段燃烧式波普独奏，以高速即兴句法和强烈的节奏冲击，为整体注入活力。值得注意的是，这两段亮眼的即兴段落成为乐评反复提及的亮点，凸显低音与乐队的张力对话。

album: Ivan Pavlov interview: ‘The book is the final Soisong release’
excerpt: Ivan Pavlov, who records as CoH, co-founded Soisong with the late Peter “Sleazy” Christopherson in Bangkok in 2007. The project produced the octagonal “Soisong EP” tour CDEP in 2008 and the full-length “xAj3z,” which documented two European tours. The project held its final concert at Hau 2 in Berlin on June 5, 2010 – without Christopherson, whose health had declined to the point that he could not fly. Christopherson died in Bangkok on November 25, 2010.
body: Ivan Pavlov, who records as CoH, co-founded Soisong with the late Peter “Sleazy” Christopherson in Bangkok in 2007. The project produced the octagonal “Soisong EP” tour CDEP in 2008 and the full-length “xAj3z,” which documented two European tours. The project held its final concert at Hau 2 in Berlin on June 5, 2010 – without Christopherson, whose health had declined to the point that he could not fly. Christopherson died in Bangkok on November 25, 2010. A 2012 event at Bar Bonobo in Tokyo, the venue where the project’s first concert had taken place, marked a symbolic close. On May 22, 2026, Pavlov released “Soisong Book” – a 160-page faux-leather hardcover limited to 222 numbered copies – through the official Soisong store. The book draws on email correspondence, private photographs, official announcements, manifestos, and items Pavlov describes as “fake documents”: promotional materials created during the project’s active years. Two CDs are affixed inside the cover: a 2007 Tokyo concert recording pre-dating Soisong’s formation, and a new studio album by trumpet player Julio Ecclesiast, who contributed to “xAj3z.” Side-Line spoke with Pavlov about the archive behind the book, the nature of some of Soisong’s listed performers, the night in Berlin, and what follows this release. Soisong interview SL: The book draws heavily on email exchanges between you and Sleazy. How large was that archive, and what guided your selection process? Were there exchanges you wanted to include but felt were too private? Ivan Pavlov: I have about a thousand emails in my mailbox filed under ‘Sleazy’, but since it’s a Soisong book, only those that relate to the process have been included. SL: You described upscaling late-2000s cellphone photos and low-res Myspace images using current technology. Where did you draw the line between restoring what was there and altering it? Did any images come out looking wrong once upscaled? Ivan Pavlov: Good upscaling algorithms do not alter images to anything one would be able to notice in print, so no, the printed images look the same as their low-res originals. SL: The book includes what you describe as “fake documents.” Can you give a specific example – were these created during the project’s active years, or produced later for the book? Ivan Pavlov: You can see them in the book. For example, as part of the campaign for Soisong album called ‘xAj3z’ we had published a so-called Report from an, obviously non-existent, Investigating Committee. The report speculated on and promoted the shape of the CD package as an extraterrestrial object, with multiple illustrations. This was all made back in 2009. SL: 222 copies is a precise figure. Is there a reason for that specific number, or was it determined by print-run economics? Ivan Pavlov: You may find in the book a rather extensive dialogue about choosing the name for the project. I won’t expand too much on that, but ‘song’ is ‘two’ in Thai language. As for the economics for any kind of small editions – it is tough, indeed. SL: The first CD captures the 2007 Tokyo concert where CoH and The Threshold House Boys Choir performed as separate acts – a pre-Soisong moment. Why that recording specifically? Was it already in the archive, or did it require sourcing? Ivan Pavlov: Back then, a few days after the show I received 2 CDs from the sound engineer who was at the main desk during the concert. One with a room recording, i.e. including the sound of the audience, one with the clean signal. I now made a mix of the two and I see it as a document well related to Soisong – in the book you will find a mention of the show, and the subsequent discussion on playing live. SL: The second CD contains a new studio album by Julio Ecclesiast, the trumpet player from “xAj3z.” How did that collaboration come about – did you approach him, or did the idea come from him? How much input did you have in the direction of his album? Ivan Pavlov: Just like several other participants in Soisong, Julio mostly exists in domains of imagination, listener’s imagination included. Which already back in 2009 had become a rather typical, important part of Soisong’s approach to choosing the performers. SL: Soisong’s packaging choices were consistently unusual – the octagonal CDEP, the warning on “xAj3z” that it could only play in CD players with a flat horizontal tray. How much of that approach came from Sleazy, and how much from you? Ivan Pavlov: I would usually come up with rough geometrical design ideas, which we then perfected through a mutually encouraging dialogue. SL: The final Soisong show took place at Hau 2 in Berlin on June 5, 2010, without Sleazy. What do you remember about that night, and what was the decision behind going ahead without him? Ivan Pavlov: There was no decision making as such, as far as I remember we were about to play a few shows in Europe, but then Sleazy’s health suddenly declined which didn’t let him fly. The show in Berlin was too late to cancel, so we went on with this kind of ‘remote version’. Sleazy recorded a video message to the audience, and a video stream for me to play during the show. I played the music. It felt quite lonely on the stage, I admit. SL: Christopherson died in Bangkok on November 25, 2010 – the city where Soisong was based. How did you decide what to do with the project’s archive after that? Was there a point where you considered closing it entirely? Ivan Pavlov: Soisong is pretty much closed ever since Sleazy’s departure. Whatever has been published afterwards – these are just echoes of the past on their way to the future. Soisong was only meant to last until 2012, so in 2012 we organised the symbolic final event at Bar Bonobo, in Tokyo. That’s where Soisong played the very first concert, commonly referred to as Test Run #7. During this final night at Bonobo in 2012, with the help of the bar’s owner Koichi Sei and a few other friends, the recording of Test Run #7 was released in a small edition of sealed Walkman CD players. Some years later, I also managed to put together the unfinished Soisong album ‘kAm1e’. Now comes the book, which is pretty much just a collection of artefacts. I believe we would have published this kind of the final statement if Sleazy was alive, too. SL: Dais Records released a remastered deluxe 2LP of “xAj3z” in 2025, with one previously unreleased track, “Lom Tum Lai Kwee.” How did that reissue come about, and what was it like returning to that material? Ivan Pavlov: Dais expressed interest in re-issuing the two Soisong releases on vinyl. I wouldn’t have been able to pull that off on my own, and the idea seemed attractive. So I agreed and we did it. As for coming back to Soisong material – be it email conversations, images or music – it always feels warm, feels like coming home. SL: You said the book’s creation was fuelled by “the same joyful enthusiasm and sense of fun as every other publication.” How would you describe Soisong’s working method to someone who only knows the music? Ivan Pavlov: Encouraging joyful enthusiasm in each other, and working with a sense of common fun – that is the only method we employed. SL: Does “Soisong Book” function as a closing document, or is there still archive material that could surface in future releases? Ivan Pavlov: The book is the final Soisong release. I might do a few more commemorative fake radio-broadcasts for soisong.bandcamp.com. I would also definitely like to work more with Julio Ecclesiast, which largely depends on how he feels about that… but officially as Soisong, there are no further releases planned. Soisong Broadcast #13 by SOISONG About Soisong Soisong was an experimental electronic music project formed in 2007 by Peter “Sleazy” Christopherson and Ivan Pavlov (CoH), based in Bangkok, Thailand. Christopherson had previously worked with Throbbing Gristle, Psychic TV, Coil, and The Threshold Houseboys Choir, while Pavlov released music under the CoH name. The project combined Pavlov’s computer-based composition with Christopherson’s work on artificial vocals and what the project described as “South Seas” instrumentation. The first release, “Soisong EP,” was an octagonal tour CDEP issued in 2008 in disposable-design packaging, with the release title doubling as a password for additional material on the project’s website. The full-length “xAj3z” followed, in octagonal packaging and carrying a warning that the disc could only play in CD players with a flat horizontal tray. Live activity included the 2008 Test Run Tour – with dates in Tokyo, Rovereto, Copenhagen, Bilbao, Amsterdam, Moscow, and Athens – and a 2009 reunion tour with shows in Linz, Moscow, St. Petersburg, Wroclaw, and Cologne. The final concert took place at Hau 2 in Berlin on June 5, 2010, performed without Christopherson. Christopherson died in Bangkok on November 25, 2010. A 2012 event at Bar Bonobo in Tokyo, site of the project’s first concert, served as a symbolic close: the recording of that original Tokyo show, Test Run #7, was issued in a small edition of sealed Walkman CD players. Pavlov subsequently assembled the unfinished album “kAm1e.” Dais Records reissued “xAj3z” as a remastered deluxe 2LP in 2025, with the previously unreleased track “Lom Tum Lai Kwee” added to the Bandcamp edition released on May 30, 2025. “Soisong Book,” released May 22, 2026, is confirmed as the final Soisong release.
_cn_summary: Soisong是由俄罗斯噪声/电子音乐人Ivan Pavlov（以CoH身份活动）与前Throbbing Gristle/Coil成员Peter“Sleazy”Christopherson于2007年在曼谷共同创立的实验项目，融合工业噪声、低频脉动与空灵的环境层，呈现冷冽、压抑且具空间感的声响。其2008年的EP以及随后收录两轮欧洲巡演的完整专辑《xAj3z》在极简结构中穿插突发的高频碎屑与密集低频冲击，形成强烈的现场能量感。值得注意的是，2024年出版的配套书籍以档案资料和访谈形式完整记录了该项目的创作历程与最后的柏林现场，突显Sleazy缺席的遗憾与两人合作的独特遗产。

body: We have Vancouver’s own Verboden Festival coming up this weekend in our backyard, and we’re excited about seeing a slew of familiar faves like SRSQ and Male Tears as well as catching acts we’ve been tracking through studio material but have yet to catch live, like Dildox and More Ephemerol. Hope to catch up with regular readers/listeners, too – should be a great weekend. On with this week’s tracks! Scimitar Street Sects, “No Percentage In Caution” The pair of LPs released by long-standing industrial punk terrorists Street Sects gave us a lot to chew on last year, and the band’s declaration that they’re moving in a “more rhythm based/song focused direction” with their new stuff is intriguing. This first sample clearly finds some of the harmonic and synth hook elements of the Full Color Eclipse second being drawn into a rhythmically tight package. No Percentage in Caution by Street Sects Sydney Valette, “I Fucking Love You” We’ve come to associate Sydney Valette with a more continental and very French take on modern darkwave, avoiding many of the cliches of the style in favour of something that feels both classic, but without being beholden to the ur sources of the sound. New single “I Fucking Love You” holds with that, but sounds more strident than any of Valette’s work in recent memory. Partly it’s the tempo and push of the song, but also it’s a distinctly wounded and gothic vocal delivery, bringing out the emotion and drama here. If this is the direction of the new record, it could signal a nice shift into a new direction that would certainly be of interest to us as fans and followers of his work. I Fucking Love You by Sydney Valette Ortrotasce, “As I See It” Ortrotasce always keeps you on your toes; from single to single and within the run-time of the occasional longer release the one-man project deigns to release you’re never exactly sure where in the sprawling fields of synthpop, EBM, darkwave, and new beat things might land. You even have to keep your head on a pivot mid-track, as the peppy, Kraftwerkian programming of this early electro number is swiftly offset by a gloomy and resigned vocal which feels wholly separate. As I See It by Ortrotasce Transmigration, “Understanding” Last we checked in with the UK’s Transmigration, we noted their capacity to make the kind of gritty dark electro that benefits from obscurity and rough edges. New cut “Understanding”, the first taster from EP Living Information isn’t a huge leap away from that aesthetic, but it’s also a lot sharper and more direct, with atmosphere evolving out of the vocals, the speedy sequences and the aggression of the delivery, almost as a byproduct. The result is one of urgency, with a lot of the power stemming from how open and direct it all is, creating a sound that doesn’t need to be dressed up at all, arriving unforced, unadorned and hard-hitting. Living Information by Transmigration Scimitar, “Zenith (Inhalt remix)” Little bit of a ID:UD twofer this week with this Scimitar remix by Inhalt. We’ll be seeing the Los Angeles based band for the first time at Verboden this coming weekend, and we’re quite keen to do so; as an act we’ve tracked for a few years, they’ve consistently put out material that defies a lot of dark alt music trends, capturing sounds that are spiky, punky and uncompromising. And (spoilers) this week’s episode of We Have a Technical has Matia Simnovich of Inhalt as a guest, talking about the art of being a producer and what that entails. Tune into the latter, and then next week to hear our impressions of the performance from the former! Zenith (Inhalt Remix) by Scimitar Nikonn feat. MeLLLo, “Lighthouse” Lastly, something fairly off-format for us but still salient to our coverage. MeLLLo, AKA Marianthi Melitsi of the on-hiatus but never far from our playlists synthpop act Marsheaux, makes a guest vocal appearance on the new single by London producer Nikonn, and her familiar, soothing tone glides perfectly over this downtempo mix of dreampop and chillout instrumentation, making us wistful for the sorts of crepuscular ballads which complemented Marsheaux’s club numbers so very nicely. body: Although primarily known as a Bach interpreter, pianist Simone Dinnerstein and her string ensemble, Baroklyn, find a natural affinity for the music of Philip Glass, the subject of Hourglass, her first recording for the Naïve label. Yet affinity alone hardly explains the uncanny sense of inevitability that permeates these performances. What emerges instead is a meeting of imaginations preoccupied with the strange elasticity of passing moments and the hidden variations between them. In the album booklet, the ensemble’s leader observes that every repetition in Glass reacts to what preceded it while anticipating what follows. Nothing remains static. “We hear it as a constant becoming,” she writes, “not as a set of musical facts.” That idea becomes the philosophical axis of the recording. More than a play on the composer’s surname, Hourglass evokes matter suspended within time’s narrowing chamber, each grain brushing against countless others on its descent. Dinnerstein approaches Glass not as a minimalist sculptor of patterns but as a composer of tides and gradual transformation. Her playing reveals an art founded on metamorphosis. The Suite from “The Hours” (2002) opens the album in a state of exquisite unease. The source material already carries the weight of fractured interior lives, yet what emerges here reaches beyond narrative into something almost cosmological. Upper and lower strings move in subtle dislocations, circling one another like celestial bodies uncertain whether they approach union or catastrophe. Beneath them, the cellos sway with a dignified grief. At the center of this emotional system burns no triumphant sun. Instead, one encounters the afterimage of a dying star, its radiance stretched thin across immeasurable distance. The musicians understand the necessity of restraint, receding whenever needed so that Dinnerstein’s piano may gather the evaporating particles left behind by the strings before they disappear into the surrounding dark. Every phrase feels suspended between touch and extinction. What astonishes most is the music’s sense of disembodiment. It hovers just beyond ordinary consciousness, brushing against intuitions the intellect cannot fully stabilize. Glass is often reduced to discussions of process and structure, yet these performances uncover something deeply organic beneath the repetitions. Each figure develops its own ecology, its own gravitational field. Dinnerstein shapes the motifs as living terrains whose contours shift under changing light. Time transforms recurrence into an altered emotional space. Every return carries traces of what came before. Meanings accumulate gradually, through accretion rather than declaration, until each phrase seems to open inward toward another hidden chamber. A passage of fluttering trills briefly alters the atmosphere. Suddenly, there are birds suspended over immense fields, flashes of earthly tenderness interrupting the work’s abstraction. Yet even these remain touched by remoteness. The violins continue drawing the listener deeper into an immense interior cosmos where emotion belongs to matter itself. Part II emerges from the husk of those earlier sorrows with newfound translucence. The strings unfold in slow waves, allowing the piano to float upon their surface as both reflection and witness. A faint harmonic shift changes the coloration of the entire landscape. The transition into Part III possesses the delicate instability of waking from a dream whose images resist immediate translation. The piano searches through ascending gestures that feel at once anxious and ceremonial. Dinnerstein renders these moments with extraordinary sensitivity to weight and spacing. She never hurries revelation, allowing uncertainty to linger long enough to become attractive. And then, the melodies release us as gently as they first gathered us. One leaves the suite with the sensation of having crossed through several seasons in a single night. The recording quality deserves particular praise. The keyboard exists both within the orchestra’s collective body and apart from it, intimate yet unreachable, a consciousness wandering among other consciousnesses. Harp and celesta enter with spectral luminosity, altering the chemistry of light itself. From there, we enter the denser terrain of the Tirol Concerto for Piano and Orchestra (2000). Ostensibly Glass’s first piano concerto, the work balances inheritance and subversion, acknowledging a grand tradition while quietly hollowing out many of its assumptions. From the opening’s shifting, sand-like textures, the listener is drawn into a landscape haunted by premonitions of Glass’s later Étude No. 13. The immense second movement forms the emotional core not only of the concerto but of the album itself. Spanning nearly 17 minutes, it unfolds with the patient majesty of something unconcerned with ordinary temporal measures. There is nothing exhibitionistic about its beauty. Few scores in Glass’s output achieve this degree of aching translucence, and the present recording approaches it with reverence unmarred by sentimentality. Midway through the movement, ascending scales rise with almost unbearable clarity. Their motion suggests release while remaining tethered to gravity. Dinnerstein articulates these passages with crystalline poise, allowing every note to refract like sunlight entering deep water. As the mood recedes into dissonance, the landscape changes once again. And by the time the final movement arrives with its dancing contours and coiling energies, joy has become inseparable from experience. Earlier shadows remain present within every gesture of exuberance. Yet Glass refuses the simplicity of triumph. Even heroism rests on the back of fragility. Such maturity gives the concerto its enduring power: resolution emerges not through conquest but through recognition that every forward motion leaves something behind. Throughout Hourglass, Dinnerstein reveals herself not merely as an interpreter of Glass but as someone capable of exposing an underlying metaphysics. Too often, discussions of his music become trapped within debates over minimalism, repetition, accessibility, or influence. This recording bypasses those exhausted categories entirely. It restores mystery to music that many listeners assume they already understand. The natural reaction to all this is not simply admiration for the performances, extraordinary as they are, but a heightened awareness of time’s strange interiority. Glass and Dinnerstein seem less interested in measuring duration than in revealing how the human soul inhabits it. The hourglass does not merely count passing grains. It transforms motion into memory. Perhaps that is why this music lingers with such unsettling force. It reminds us that identity itself may consist of endlessly repeated patterns altered by the invisible pressures surrounding us. We return to familiar thoughts, believing them to be unchanged, only to discover they now contain the dreams of another life. Hourglass is set for release on June 5. body: Review by The Progolyte — Gleemen was one of the first Rock Progressivo Italiano groups to ever come out, with their one and only record of the seventies, their self-titled, coming out all the way back in 1970. I obviously got attracted to this record from its very strange album cover, which depicts some sort of creature being killed and stabbed by various other creatures and is an ugly yet captivating piece of art. Moving on, while this band is listed as Rock Progressivo Italiano on ProgArchives, it's more or less just trippy hard rock with some symphonic textures added to it, with minimal details going beyond just a few cool riffs and a slightly interesting rhythm sections and various solos. One of the main things I didn't like about this record was the vocals, which on my first listen I thought sounded a lot like what Garybaldi was doing in their albums, and I thought it was just a coincidence until I noticed that the two bands were actually related and shared some of the same personnel (it's actually basically the same personnel as Garybaldi in the seventies. Moving on to the music, so with the band being related to Garybaldi, you can obviously tell that there will be some similarities to their music. Now, it's not that I dislike Garybaldi, I just think they're a B-tier band, so I was thinking the I Gleemen would be the same once I found out they were essentially the same band, just with a different name and in different years. And I was right. The music here is quite bland and doesn't have very many good details and is quite simple and normal in the grand scheme of things when you look at the Rock Progressivo Italiano bands that would come out in the following years. Now don't get me wrong, I do respect Gleemen for being one of the first Italian bands to release an album exploring this musical direction and something similar to the classic heavier symphonic prog sound of Rock Progressivo Italiano, they just lack the energy, excitement, depth, and complexity of others. However, some of the music here was still memorable and had some nice touches that made it flow nicely. In conclusion, Gleemen will most likely remain as the forgotten origins of Garybaldi and never get any big recognition within the progressive rock community (or even in the Rock Progressivo Italiano community), but at least they tried, and the one album they put out was alright. This one is a mid 3/5.
_cn_summary: Gleemen是意大利七十年代最早一批摇滚先锋（Rock Progressivo Italiano）乐队之一，仅在1970年发行过唯一一张同名专辑，因而被视为RPI史上的稀缺先驱。该专辑的声音以厚重的哈蒙德风琴、低沉的贝斯线条以及结构稍显松散的长篇编曲为特征，融合了早期意大利民谣旋律与现代摇滚的即兴冲动，呈现出原始而略带稚拙的先锋气质。封面那幅残忍而奇异的生物杀戮图成为唱片最抢眼的视觉标签，而专辑因制作粗糙、曲目罕见在当代乐迷中拥有极高的收藏价值和研究意义。

body:
Valerio Cairone — Kairos (self-released Novee Arte Lab, 2025)

Italian vocalist, composer, multi-instrumentalist and “sound painter” Valerio Cairone released his first solo album, Kairos, in 2025. The recording features 11 tracks that Cairone describes as “sympho-electro-acoustic poems.” The title references the ancient Greek distinction between kairos (qualitative, opportune time) and chronos, or linear, measurable time.

Cairone’s music crackles—whoosh, thrum, shimmer—as circuitry collides with ancestral sound. He chanels the raw, molten spirit of Mount Etna and the sun-drenched charm of Sicily. His Etad vision (Electronic Traditional Acoustic Dance) erupts, fusing folktronica warmth with psybient vapor into something fiercely alive.

Each track persuades and sparks, hypnotic, inviting, as delicate electronic beats pulse beneath a lush canopy of transformed acoustic instruments. Strings, drums, reeds… are warped, stretched, and electrified into glowing new forms.

The Sicilian musician completed studies in Music Education at the Bellini Conservatory in Catania and in Film Score Composition at the Conservatory of Rovigo. His career has since reached stages in India, South America, Australia, and Europe.

Kairos follows his acclaimed work on diatonic accordion and Sicilian bagpipes with Oi Dipnoi on Bastrika (2015) and Pontos (2018), and was made after a period of retreat and research.

Cairone plays bagpipes, Hungarian and Sicilian jaw harps, sarangi, tabla, cello, accordions, melodeons, piano, soprano saxophone, trumpet, bansuri, double flutes, ethnic flutes, computer, khamak, voice, Tibetan bell, eastern cymbals, ocarinas, guitars, frame, drums, Sicilian castanets, and synthesizers.

Buy Kairos.
_cn_summary: Valerio Cairone 是一位意大利的声乐、作曲、多乐器演奏者兼“声绘”概念艺术家，首张个人专辑《Kairos》在2025年由独立厂牌 Novee Arte Lab 发行。专辑以实验性声景、氛围电子与即兴演唱交织的手法，营造出层层叠加的音场与细腻的声线变化。最值得关注的是他将现场器乐、电子音效与声乐即兴融合的“声绘”手法，使作品在结构与情感层面均呈现独特的张力。

body: South Korean indie favourites JANNABI are finally heading to Singapore for the very first time. Presented by FriedRice Entertainment, the duo’s JANNABI 1st Asia Tour : Sweat & Stardust in Singapore will take place on 13 August at Capitol Theatre, marking the Singapore stop of the band’s first-ever Asia tour. Comprised of Choi Jung-hoon and Kim Do-hyung, JANNABI have become one of Korea’s most beloved indie acts thanks to their nostalgic chamber pop sound and emotionally resonant songwriting. Since debuting in 2014, the band have steadily built a devoted following through releases that explore themes of youth, love, and growth. View this post on Instagram A post shared by FriedRice Entertainment (@friedrice.live) The band are perhaps best known for their breakout hit ‘for lovers who hesitate’, which took home Song of the Year at the 17th Korean Music Awards in 2020. Their live performances have also earned acclaim for their immersive storytelling and distinct concepts, with their futuristic concert All the Boys and Girls 2125 winning the Grand Prize for Best Concert at the 12th EDAILY Culture Awards. Fans attending the Singapore show can also look forward to exclusive fan benefits. VIP ticket holders will receive priority entry to the standing pen, priority merchandise access, a JANNABI guitar pick, and a chance to win a signed concert poster. All ticket holders will also receive a commemorative postcard. Tickets go on sale from 2 PM (SGT) on 3 June via Ticketmaster Singapore.
_cn_summary: JANNABI（崔正勋、金度亨）是韩国 indie 双人组合，以怀旧 chamber pop 为基底、兼具复古吉他扫弦与细腻弦乐编排著称，情感真挚的歌词是其核心吸引力。此次「Sweat & Stardust」亚洲巡演在新加坡 Capitol Theatre 首演，将现场再现其温暖合唱、层次分明的编曲以及充满叙事性的现场氛围，是乐迷不可错过的现场体验。

body: Looking back on a glorious 11-year journey, the sun isn't setting anytime soon on SEVENTEEN as they celebrate their anniversary, sharing warm and heartfelt messages with CARATs on Weverse. Earlier this year, S.Coups, Jeonghan, Joshua, Jun, Hoshi, Wonwoo, Woozi, DK, Mingyu, The8, Seungkwan, Vernon, and Dino all renewed their contracts with PLEDIS Entertainment, strengthening their bond with fans as they make a pledge to be their favourite idols for as long as they can. With many more milestone anniversaries on the horizon, CARATs celebrate this landmark moment by sharing clips of old performances and iconic moments that stay etched in their minds. As fans reminisce about the journey of the group so far, the members took to Weverse to share their messages of appreciation, joining in on the nostalgic reflection of the paths they've forged. Although he is currently serving his national service, Hoshi expresses his excitement to complete his duties and reunite with the band to continue performing and creating new bangers for fans to rock out to. The8 echoes a similar sentiment as he expresses his love by saying, "It’s been 11 years. Thank you for always being by our side, thank you to all the members for getting this far, it hasn’t been easy. Because of the time we’ve spent together, we've long become a part of each other’s lives. We hope to continue creating many more memories together in the future. Thank you for your unwavering love." As each member expresses their gratitude for the support from CARATs for the past 11 years, they look forward to an even more eventful future as SEVENTEEN. The group anticipates more new hits, even bigger performances, and new endeavours as they continue to preserve the original energy and passion that they have served up since their debut.

body: Lola Amour celebrated a decade of music with a sold-out two-night anniversary event at 123 Block in Mandaluyong on 22 and 23 May, drawing over 2,500 fans across the weekend for a heartfelt full-circle celebration of the band’s journey. Originally planned as a one-night show on 23 May, overwhelming demand prompted the addition of a “Pre-Game” night on 22 May — with both dates eventually selling out. Across the two evenings, fans were treated to performances from Any Name’s Okay, Jan Roberts, Shirebound, and The Ridleys, alongside a career-spanning set from Lola Amour themselves. Beyond the live performances, attendees also explored the Lola Amour Museum, an exhibit showcasing memorabilia from the band’s 10-year history. Among the featured pieces were the band’s 2017 Wanderband Champions trophy, their Japan Ruby Award from the 2025 Music Awards Japan, and the iconic “Shiela” costume from the ‘Raining in Manila’ music video. The anniversary weekend was packed with memorable moments that highlighted the band’s close relationship with its fans and collaborators. One standout performance saw Sof of Any Name’s Okay join the band for ‘Clarity’, while a chaotic and crowd-pleasing cover of ‘Mr. Brightside’ brought together Jan Roberts, Renzo of Any Name’s Okay, Ivo Impreso of PLAYERTWO, and former road manager Peter onstage. During the set, bassist Manu crowd-surfed through the audience, earning one of the loudest cheers of the weekend. Fans also witnessed a playful moment during ‘Lambing’, where frontman Pio transformed into a human disco ball with a mirrored helmet during the song’s instrumental break. The emotional high point of the celebration came during a reunion of the bands that would eventually form Lola Amour. Former members Raymond King and Martin Kim returned to perform as Decaf, while current trumpeter Angelo Mesina briefly returned to his original role as drummer. Joxx Perez and Renzo Santos also made surprise appearances as Sinigang Na Baboy. To close the weekend, all former members joined Lola Amour onstage for the final chorus of ‘Raining in Manila’, creating a powerful moment that encapsulated the band’s decade-long journey from playing small venues to becoming one of the Philippines’ biggest acts. Part concert, part reunion, and part tribute to the community that has supported them since the beginning, Lola Amour’s anniversary weekend felt less like a retrospective and more like a celebration of everything still ahead for the band.

body: RIIZE keep their musical momentum going as they soar into a warm and summery new chapter with their upcoming album II, hitting the charts on 15 June. Following the successful release of their debut full-length album ODYSSEY, the sextet explores a new sonic direction with this project, reinforcing their versatility with each release. Spanning six tracks, II is a statement of raw artistic authenticity with a straightforward message that emphasises the importance of staying true to yourself. At the heart of the album is the title track 'Do Your Dance', that doubles down on the key message of the album while blending their signature musicality with layered sonic textures and evocative storytelling through the lyrics. RIIZE empower fans, telling them to own their spotlight with confidence through the signature vocals that have defined the group's sound, delivered with the maturity of a group entering its fourth year. RIIZE unveiled an official schedule detailing each upcoming release as part of the mini album. Fans can look forward to the string of teaser content, including trailer videos and images, a preview of the title track, and music video teasers set for release from 25 May onwards, leading up to the record's release on 15 June. With II, RIIZE continue to cement their place as one of K-pop’s most exciting rising acts, balancing experimentation with the signature sound that fans have come to love. As anticipation builds toward the album’s release, the project promises to usher in another defining era for the group, one fuelled by confidence, growth, and a fearless embrace of their evolving artistry.

body: Dikke tien jaar na zijn eerste soloalbum (“Filth Haven” op Malignant Records, 2015) keert de experimentele muzikant en sounddesigner Kristoffer Oustad uit het Noorse Arendal terug met "Magnor", deze keer op het Poolse Zoharum label. Kristoffer Oustad heeft al een gevarieerde muzikale carrière achter de rug, beginnend met extreme metal in de black/death/industrial metal projecten V:O:I:D en V:28, voordat hij zich meer op experimentele muziek en sounddesign begon te richten. “Magnor” (7 tracks, 45 minuten speelduur) klinkt als een filmische, gelaagde en ijzige ontdekkingsreis door dark ambient en industriële muziek. Het album zit geworteld in klassieke industrial- en dark ambient-tradities (vooral de typisch Scandinavische), maar met een zeer persoonlijke benadering. De kern van het album is het thema van spirituele verbondenheid of een kompas in de leegte. Het album nodigt je expliciet uit om die ijzige leegte te betreden, met de muziek zelf als je enige kompas. De albumtitel is ontleend aan een Noors grensplaatsje. Voor Oustad is Magnor niet zomaar een geografische locatie. Het staat symbool voor een fysieke plek, een richting én een specifieke gemoedstoestand. De muziek onderzoekt de intense relatie tussen Oustad en de ruwe, onherbergzame Scandinavische natuur die zijn identiteit vormt. Het album ademt een sfeer van eenzaamheid, nostalgie en geografische isolatie. "Magnor" is gecomponeerd en gerijpt over meerdere jaren, met behulp van analoge en modulaire synthesizers, minimale nabewerking en een sterke focus op structuur, dynamiek en sfeer, met zeer weinig digitale opsmuk achteraf. De muziek werd live ingespeeld, eerder dan strak voorgeprogrammeerd, wat het een gevoel van aanwezigheid en authenticiteit verleent en een cruciaal onderdeel vormt van het karakter van het album. Voor het album maakte Oustad intensief gebruik van analoge effecten, diepe drones en korrelige ruis. “Magnor” vraagt om geduld van de luisteraar, maar beloont die met een diepe en meeslepende luisterervaring. De nummers ademen een ijzige, desolate Scandinavische sfeer en doen zeer filmisch aan. “White Sacred Arrow” zet als openingsnummer direct de toon en is met een lengte van bijna tien minuten de langste compositie op het album. Het nummer fungeert als de poort naar de ijzige, desolate wereld van “Magnor”. Het is de kompasnaald die naar het Noorden wijst. Het begint extreem minimalistisch met diepe, pulserende bassen, die aanvoelen als een gure wind over een desolaat Noors landschap. Oustad dwingt de luisteraar tot geduld. Pas na enkele minuten transformeren de minimale drones zich via analoge synthesizers in een zware, tastbare muur van geluid en subtiele melodie. Het weerspiegelt perfect het centrale albumthema van een spirituele zoektocht of een kompas in de leegte. Mijn favoriet en de absolute uitschieter van het album is ongetwijfeld de tweede track “The Beacon”, met quasi continu gekraak over de enigmatische, dreigende en stikdonkere ambient klanken. Het nummer vormt een direct, logisch vervolg op de ijzige openingstrack. Het brengt een subtiele verschuiving in de dynamiek van het album en fungeert als een baken (beacon) in de leegte: De titel sluit naadloos aan bij het centrale albumthema van een spirituele zoektocht en de metafoor van het album als een kompas in de duisternis en leegte. Waar de eerste track je achterlaat in een desolaat, ijskoud landschap, fungeert dit nummer als een sonisch lichtpunt of oriëntatiepunt waar de luisteraar naartoe wordt getrokken. Ook hier wordt gebruik gemaakt van modulaire synthesizers. Het nummer drijft op langgerekte, diepe analoge drones die gestaag pulseren. In plaats van een abrupte climax te zoeken, blijft het nummer hangen in een constante, hypnotiserende staat van spanning. De overgang vanuit de ijzige rust van de eerste track naar de meer abstracte, minimalistische geluidsstructuren van de volgende tracks (zoals “A Consequence Of Entropy”, “Bring Back The Wolves” en “The Gravity Of Colour”) wordt hiermee perfect ingezet. "A Consequence Of Entropy": entropie – zo weten we nog uit de lessen fysica en thermodynamica - staat voor chaos en het langzaam vervallen van systemen. Dit sluit aan bij de melancholie van een verlaten grensstreek waar de tijd lijkt stil te staan en de natuur de menselijke sporen langzaam terugwint. Het nummer "Bring Back The Wolves", de middelste track, de vierde van zeven, kan gezien worden als het absolute, angstaanjagende hoogtepunt en de muzikale climax van de plaat. Het roept het ruwe, gevaarlijke en pure Scandinavische verleden op. Het staat symbool voor het terugkeren naar de basis en de herintroductie van de wilde natuur in de leegte. In “The Gravity Of Colour”, de vijfde track, zit een dialoog tussen een man en een vrouw. “The Gravity Of Color” hint naar hoe zwaar de grauwe, monochrome kleuren van het Noorse winterlandschap op de menselijke psyche kunnen drukken, zoals een winterdepressie in de lange poolnacht. “Magnetic Blood” vormt als voorlaatste nummer de opmaat naar de ontknoping (“Detachment”). De titel verraadt het al: het nummer heeft een ‘magnetische’, dwingende, hypnotiserende aantrekkingskracht. Je hoort hier weer duidelijk de live ingespeelde, modulaire synthesizers. Er zit een constante, onderhuidse spanning en ritmische puls in die doet denken aan een kloppende hartslag of stromend bloed door de aderen. "Magnetic Blood" is qua songtitel de meest directe verwijzing naar de onlosmakelijke, spirituele binding met een plek. De aantrekkingskracht van de Heimat zit de artiest letterlijk in het bloed, alsof een intern kompas hem er altijd naar terugtrekt. "Detachment" vormt de absolute, conceptuele ontknoping van de plaat. Waar het album begint met een zoektocht, staat dit laatste nummer volledig in het teken van de betekenis van de titel: loslating en onthechting. Meest opvallend is hier het poëtische spoken word door Jonathan Grieve, bekend van het Britse ambient-industrial en experimental project Contrastate. Zijn indringende spoken word, waarin de songtitel regelmatig terugkeert, snijdt diep door de muziek heen. Dit geeft het nummer een menselijke, maar tegelijkertijd spookachtige en theatrale lading. Muzikaal gezien fungeert de track als de emotionele nasleep. De dwingende, mechanische hartslag uit de voorgaande track, “Magnetic Blood”, is hier weggeëbd. Wat overblijft is een ijle, melancholische en mistige soundscape. De analoge drones zwellen nog één keer aan om een getormenteerde, desolate sfeer neer te zetten. Daarna lossen ze langzaam op in het niets. Het nummer laat de luisteraar achter met een onbehaaglijk, maar sereen gevoel van berusting. Met “Detachment” sluit Kristoffer Oustad de cirkel van zijn spirituele en muzikale kompas. De intense industriële spanning maakt definitief plaats voor pure, ijzige leegte. https://oustad.bandcamp.com Magnor by Kristoffer Oustad
_cn_summary: 克里斯托弗·奥斯特（Kristoffer Oustad）是来自挪威阿恩达尔的实验音乐人与声音设计师，曾在黑/死亡/工业金属项目V:O:I:D与V:28中奠定极端金属背景，十年后于2023年通过波兰厂牌Zoharum发行个人第二张专辑《Magnor》，全长约45分钟、共7曲。专辑延续其金属根源，却在声音构建上大量融入工业噪音、无人机与暗潮氛围，以厚重的纹理层叠和尖锐的噪声冲击对比空灵的延音空间，形成高度结构化的实验声景。值得注意之处在于其精准的声音设计与在激烈噪声与细致氛围之间的动态平衡，使《Magnor》在噪声实验与暗色氛围的交叉点上极具辨识度。

excerpt: Looking for a gig where you can let loose after a long week at work? Or do you require a fresh idea for a weekend date with that special someone in your life? With a variety of live music events already added to the 2026 calendar, you can rest assured that you will find something that suits your needs.
